:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y = v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^{2} + 3y^{2}}{2xy}$

Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{xy}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because it is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y),
$$

and we notice that all terms in the numerator and denominator of $f(x,y)$ are of order $2$ (i.e., they are quadratic).

Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{xy} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{2}-{x}^{2}}{x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}-1)}{v{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{2}-1}{v}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{2}-1-{v}^{2}}{v} \\ v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int v\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+C{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{yx}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{yx}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)x}{(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{v{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v}{{v}^{2}+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v-{v}^{3}-v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{{v}^{3}})\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{2{v}^{2}} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{y}{x}|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{y}{x}|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =C \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because it is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y),
$$

and we notice that all terms in the numerator and denominator of $f(x,y)$ are of order $3$ (i.e., they are cubic).

Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{3}+x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}(vx)+{x}^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}(vx)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}({v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1)}{{x}^{3}({v}^{2}+v)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1}{{v}^{2}+v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1}{{v}^{2}+v}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1-{v}^{3}-{v}^{2}}{{v}^{2}+v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v+1}{v(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int v\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+1)
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{vx}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{vx}{x}\right)+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =v\operatorname{ln}⁡v+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =v\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

To evaluate the integral on the left-hand side, we use integration by substitution with

$$
u=\operatorname{ln}⁡v,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=\frac{1}{v}.
$$

We now proceed to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{u}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|u| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡v| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡v| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{C} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{C}|x|) \\ |\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =|x|{e}^{C} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x} & =\pm {e}^{C}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x} & =Kx \\ \frac{y}{x} & ={e}^{Kx} \\ y & =x{e}^{Kx}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced the new constant of integration:

$$
K=\pm {e}^{C}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}}.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}{x}^{3}}{({v}^{2}+1){x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}-{v}^{3}-v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (v+\frac{1}{v})\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡|v| & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({v}^{2}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\right) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}) & =C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =C-\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}) \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{C-\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2})} & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}+(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}(1+{v}^{3})}{{v}^{2}{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1+{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1}{{v}^{2}}+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} \\ {v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {v}^{2}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{3}}{3}\,\text{d}v & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+3{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have let $C=3{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C) \\ y & =x\sqrt[3]{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+2y}{x}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x+2(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x(1+2v)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =1+2v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =1+v \\ \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{1+v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{C}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{C}_{1}}|x|) \\ |v+1| & ={e}^{{C}_{1}}|x| \\ v+1 & =\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}x \\ v+1 & =Cx \\ v & =Cx-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have let $C=\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & =Cx-1 \\ y & =C{x}^{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x}
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x+(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x(1+v)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =1+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ v & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+Cx.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a homogeneous equation because it is written in the form

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}+yx+{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{2}+(vx)x+{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}+v+1)}{{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & ={v}^{2}+v+1-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & ={v}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{1}{{v}^{2}+1}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{v}^{2}+1}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{v}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(v) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ v & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C) \\ y & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following differential equations are homogeneous?

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
    =
    f(x, y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero, meaning that it satisfies

$$
f(tx, ty) = f(x, y).
$$

With that in mind, let's take a look at the right-hand side function in each differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation I is a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$ is *not* a homogeneous function of degree $0.$ Rather, it is a homogeneous function of degree $-1\mathbin{:}$
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{{t}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot f(x,y) \\  & ={t}^{-1}f(x,y)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation II is *not* a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{ty}{2(tx)}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}}\right) \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot 2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{y}{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation III is a homogenous differential equation.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given any homogeneous first-order ordinary differential equation, we can always transform it into a separable equation through the substitution $y=vx,$ where $v=v(x)$ is a function of $x.$

To understand why, suppose we have a homogeneous first-order ordinary differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
    =
    f(x, y).
$$

Then because $f$ is homogeneous of degree zero, we have

$$
f(tx, ty) = f(x, y)
$$

for any $t.$ By letting $t=\dfrac{1}{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =f(tx,ty) \\  & =f(\frac{1}{x}\cdot x,\frac{1}{x}\cdot y) \\  & =f(1,\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

where the function $F$ is defined as $F(v) = f(1,v).$ 

Now, letting $v = \dfrac{y}{x}$ (or equivalently, $y=vx$), we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(vx) & =F(v) \\ v+x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =F(v).\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is now separable! We can separate the variables as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =F(v)-v \\ \frac{1}{F(v)-v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Proof That Homogeneous First-Order Differential Equations Can Always Be Made Separable

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider the homogeneous differential equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{x+y}{x} \,.
$$

This differential equation cannot be solved using separation of variables. So, how can we solve it?

Given any homogeneous differential equation, if we substitute $y=vx$ where $v=v(x)$ is a function of $x,$ then we can transform the differential equation into one that is separable.

Differentiating the substitution $y=vx,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the original differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x+vx}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =1+v \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

The differential equation above is separable! We can solve it by integrating both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ v & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  substituting $y=v x$  we obtain the solution to the original differential equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =vx \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C)x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+Cx\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
If we're given a differential equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = f(x,y),
$$

and the right-hand side is a **homogeneous function of degree zero**, meaning that it satisfies 

$$
f(tx,ty) = f(x,y),
$$

then we say that the differential equation is a **homogeneous differential equation**.

For instance, let's take a look at the following differential equation:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}
$$

This differential equation is homogeneous. Here's why:

- Both the numerator and denominator of the function on the right-hand side are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$

- So, the rational function on the right-hand side is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2 = 0.$

- Since the right-hand side is a homogeneous function of degree $0,$ the differential equation is homogeneous.

By contrast, the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{x^3-y^3}{x^2+y^2}
$$

is *not* a homogeneous differential equation. Although the function on the right-hand side is homogeneous, its degree is $1,$ not zero.

**Watch out!** In this context, the word homogeneous refers only to the function $f(x,y)$ being a homogeneous function of degree zero. It does *not* mean the same thing as a homogeneous linear differential equation (such as one with zero forcing term). These are completely different uses of the word homogeneous, even though they share the same name.

A differential equation can be homogeneous in this sense without being linear, and a linear differential equation can be homogeneous without being homogeneous in this sense. Always check which definition is being used.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following differential equations are homogeneous?

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
    =
    f(x, y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero, meaning that it satisfies

$$
f(tx, ty) = f(x, y).
$$

With that in mind, let's take a look at the right-hand side function in each differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation I is a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$ is *not* a homogeneous function of degree $0.$ Rather, it is a homogeneous function of degree $-1\mathbin{:}$
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{{t}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot f(x,y) \\  & ={t}^{-1}f(x,y)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation II is *not* a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{ty}{2(tx)}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}}\right) \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot 2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{y}{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation III is a homogenous differential equation.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.
$$

We can express the solution in the form $y = y(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = 2C.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' + 2xy = 0$ for $y\neq 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y = y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = e^C$  and $K > 0.$ 

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y = Ke^{-x^2}.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that $x,y \geq 0,$ separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  \sqrt{2x} \cdot  \sqrt{y}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{y} \\ y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+2K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C= 2K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
y^2 = x^2 + C .
$$
